msItem.incipit: If to be great, or good deserve the bays

abstract.p: The poem praises John Davenant by stating that both greatness and goodness were recognised in him. It notes that he had several key blessings: children by a virtuous wife, good friends, and an honourable and peaceful burial. It presents his life as complete and lacking nothing. The final lines turn to the reader, urging them to reflect on their own past sins and to learn from Davenant’s example how to live and die properly.

lg.head: On the same
lg.l: If to bee Greate, or Good deserve the Baies
What merits hee whom Great and Good doth praise?
What meritts Hee? Why, a contented life,
A happy yssue of a vertuous wife,
The choyce of Freinds, a quiet honour’d Grave;
All these hee had: what more could Davnanthave
Reader go home, and with a weeping eie
For thy Sinns past, learne thus to live, and die.

div.head: Historical context and dating
div.p: John Davenant (1565–1622), vintner and proprietor of the Crown Inn, Cornmarket Street, Oxford was elected mayor on 17 September 1621. The Davenants were well-known, they kept an important inn frequented by Shakespeare, and their son William became a prominent dramatist.
